questions.prompt: You have one hour to fix the interview checks from weeks 1–8 that you marked as weak. Which way of spending it does the learning research best support, if you want to still answer them next week?

choices.text: Reread your notes on each marked topic two or three times
Highlight the key sentences in each topic's Material
Rewatch one video per marked topic from start to finish
Answer each marked question from memory, check it, and repeat the misses

questions.explanation: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated practice testing, meaning retrieving answers from memory, as high utility. They rated rereading and highlighting as low utility. In the study by Roediger and Karpicke (2006) that they describe, students who took a practice recall test remembered 56% a week later, against 42% for students who restudied the text instead. Rereading feels productive because the text looks familiar, but recognising something is not the same as being able to produce the answer in an interview.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. rate practice testing high utility and rereading and highlighting low utility, and report Roediger and Karpicke (2006b), where one-week free recall was 56% after a practice test versus 42% after restudy.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise is to answer each marked question out loud until the answer takes under two minutes. Explain why that works better than rereading your notes, and what the drill also tells you about your weak spots.

model_answer.summary: Answering from memory is practice testing, one of the two techniques the research rates highest. Rereading is rated low. The drill also shows you exactly which checks you still can't answer.
key_points: Retrieving an answer from memory strengthens later recall (the testing effect)
Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate practice testing high utility and rereading low utility
In the Roediger and Karpicke study, a practice test beat restudying one week later (56% vs 42% recall)
Saying the answer out loud shows which checks you can't yet answer cleanly, so the next round targets only those

questions.explanation: The interview is itself a recall test, so practise the same thing: producing the answer without the notes in front of you. Rereading builds familiarity, which feels like knowing but doesn't carry over well to a delayed test.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology (Dunlosky et al., 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1))
sources.claim: Dunlosky et al. rate practice testing high utility and rereading low utility, citing one-week recall of 56% after a practice test versus 42% after restudying.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

a = add_tag("x")
b = add_tag("y")
print(a, b, a is b)
```

choices.text: `['x'] ['y'] False`

questions.explanation: The default list is created once, when `def` runs, and every call that leaves out `tags` gets that same list. The first call appends `"x"` and returns the list. The second appends `"y"` to the same list and returns it again. So `a` and `b` are one object: both print `['x', 'y']`, and `a is b` is `True`. The tempting `['x'] ['x', 'y']` is wrong because `a` is not a snapshot. It is the same list, which the second call changed.

sources.title: 8. Compound statements - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Python evaluates default parameter values once, when the def statement executes, so a mutable default list modified by one call is the same object seen by later calls.

sources.title: Facts and myths about Python names and values | Ned Batchelder
sources.claim: Batchelder explains that several names can refer to one mutable object, so a change through one name is visible through all of them.

questions.prompt: Which version of `add_tag` gives each call that leaves out `tags` its own new list, and still appends to a list the caller passes in?

choices.text: `def add_tag(tag, tags=None):` then `if tags is None: tags = []` before appending
`def add_tag(tag, tags=list()):` so a fresh list is built for each call
`def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):` with `tags.clear()` as the first line of the body
`def add_tag(tag, tags=()):` so the default is immutable and can't be shared

questions.explanation: The `None` sentinel works because the new list is created inside the body, which runs on every call. `tags=list()` is still evaluated only once, when `def` runs, so it has the same bug. `tags.clear()` would also wipe a list the caller passed in. A tuple default has no `append` method, so the body would raise `AttributeError`.

sources.title: 8. Compound statements - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Python's docs recommend using None as the default and creating the new list inside the function body, because default expressions are evaluated only once at definition time.

sources.title: Built-in Types - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Python's built-in types docs list append as a mutable-sequence operation; tuples are immutable sequences without it.

sources.title: Built-in Exceptions - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Python raises AttributeError when an attribute reference fails, such as calling append on a tuple.

questions.prompt: `fail_fast()` raises `ValueError` after 0.1 s. `fetch_a()` and `fetch_c()` each take 2 s. What happens with `results = await asyncio.gather(fetch_a(), fail_fast(), fetch_c())`?

choices.text: `gather` waits the full 2 s, then raises an `ExceptionGroup`
`ValueError` reaches the caller at about 0.1 s; `fetch_a` and `fetch_c` keep running
`ValueError` reaches the caller at about 0.1 s, and the other two are cancelled
`results` is a list with the `ValueError` object in position 1

questions.explanation: With the default `return_exceptions=False`, `gather` passes the first exception straight to the awaiting code. The Python docs say the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". Cancelling the rest on failure is what `TaskGroup` does, and `TaskGroup` is also the one that raises an `ExceptionGroup`. Exceptions only appear in the results list if you pass `return_exceptions=True`.

sources.title: Coroutines and tasks - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: With return_exceptions=False, asyncio.gather propagates the first raised exception immediately to the awaiting task, and the other awaitables are not cancelled and continue to run.

questions.prompt: Your agent runs three tool calls at once and one of them fails. Compare what `asyncio.gather` and `asyncio.TaskGroup` do with the other two, and say when you would pick each.

model_answer.summary: By default `gather` raises the first error at once and leaves the other tasks running. `TaskGroup` (Python 3.11+) cancels the rest and raises an `ExceptionGroup`. Use `TaskGroup` when the calls must all succeed, and `gather(return_exceptions=True)` when you want partial results.
key_points: `gather` with the default `return_exceptions=False` raises the first exception immediately, and the other awaitables are not cancelled
`gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` returns exceptions as items in the results list, so you can keep the calls that succeeded
`TaskGroup` (Python 3.11+) cancels the remaining tasks when one fails with anything other than `CancelledError`
`TaskGroup` raises an `ExceptionGroup` after all tasks finish, which you handle with `except*`
Pick `TaskGroup` for all-or-nothing work (no orphaned tasks), and `gather(return_exceptions=True)` when each tool result is useful on its own

questions.explanation: The Python docs say `TaskGroup` gives stronger safety guarantees than `gather`, because it cancels the remaining tasks and `gather` does not. An agent that uses plain `gather` can leave tool calls running, and spending money, after the step has already failed.

sources.title: Coroutines and tasks - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: gather does not cancel other awaitables on failure and with return_exceptions=True returns exceptions in the results list; TaskGroup (3.11+) cancels remaining tasks when one fails and raises an ExceptionGroup, giving stronger safety guarantees.

questions.prompt: An agent calling the Claude API puts `Current time: <ISO timestamp>` on the first line of its system prompt, and puts a `cache_control` breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. The tool definitions never change. What happens to prompt caching?

choices.text: Only the timestamp line is reprocessed; the rest of the system prompt is a cache hit
It hits, because the system prompt is cached separately from the tool definitions
It hits for five minutes, then misses once the cache lifetime runs out
Every request misses, because the prefix up to the breakpoint is never identical

questions.explanation: A cache hit needs the prompt to be 100% identical up to and including the block marked with `cache_control`. The prefix is `tools`, then `system`, then `messages`, so a changing first line of the system prompt makes each request's prefix new. Each request then pays to write the cache and never reads it back. Nothing is cached line by line. Move the timestamp after the breakpoint, for example into the user turn.

sources.title: Prompt caching - Claude Platform Docs
sources.claim: Anthropic's docs say cache hits need 100% identical prompt segments up to and including the cache_control block, with the prefix ordered tools, system, messages.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How does prompt caching work, and what invalidates the cache?" Answer for the Claude API, and say how you would order a long agent prompt to get hits.

model_answer.summary: The cache stores a prompt prefix, in the order tools, system, messages, and a hit needs that prefix to be identical up to the `cache_control` breakpoint. A change at one level invalidates that level and every level after it. So put stable content first and anything that changes per request last.
key_points: The cached prefix is built in the order `tools` → `system` → `messages`
A hit needs the prompt to be 100% identical up to and including the block marked with `cache_control`
Changing the tool definitions invalidates the whole cache (tools, system and messages)
Stable content (tools, system prompt, fixed documents) goes before the breakpoint; timestamps and the new user turn go after it
The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes and is refreshed each time the cache is used; a 1-hour option costs more to write

questions.explanation: Checked against Anthropic's prompt-caching docs as of September 2026. The docs also list smaller triggers: changing `tool_choice` or adding or removing images keeps the tools and system cache but invalidates the messages cache. Cache writes cost more than base input tokens and cache reads cost much less, so a prefix that never repeats makes you pay more, not less.

sources.title: Prompt caching - Claude Platform Docs
sources.claim: Anthropic's docs describe the tools-system-messages prefix order, that changing tool definitions invalidates all cache levels while tool_choice or image changes invalidate only the messages cache, and a 5-minute default TTL refreshed on use with a pricier 1-hour option.

questions.prompt: By the definitions in Anthropic's "Building effective agents", which task is the best fit for an agent rather than a workflow?

choices.text: Translate each support ticket into English, then route it to one of five queues
Fix a GitHub issue in an unfamiliar repository, where the files to change aren't known in advance
Write marketing copy, check it against a brand checklist, then translate it
Extract the same eight fields from invoices that all share one layout

questions.explanation: Anthropic defines workflows as LLMs and tools run through predefined code paths. In agents, the LLM directs its own process and tool use. Agents suit open-ended problems where you can't predict the number of steps or hardcode a path, and coding agents are the article's main example. The other three tasks have a fixed, known sequence of steps, so a workflow (prompt chaining or routing) is cheaper and more predictable.

sources.title: Building Effective AI Agents
sources.claim: Anthropic defines workflows as LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths and agents as LLMs directing their own process, suited to open-ended problems where steps can't be predicted, with a coding agent for GitHub issues as the example.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "Workflow or agent: how do you decide for a given problem?" Give your answer.

model_answer.summary: Start with the simplest thing that works. Use a workflow when the steps are known, and an agent only when the path can't be predicted, because agents trade cost, latency and predictability for flexibility.
key_points: A workflow runs LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; an agent lets the LLM decide its own steps and tool use
Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it measurably helps
Agents fit open-ended tasks where the number of steps can't be predicted or hardcoded
Agents cost more and can compound errors, so they need guardrails such as a maximum number of iterations and testing in a sandbox

questions.explanation: Anthropic's article says agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and that workflows give predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks. A strong answer names the trade-off and the guardrails, not only the definitions.

sources.title: Building Effective AI Agents
sources.claim: Anthropic advises starting with the simplest solution, notes agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, and recommends testing in sandboxes with guardrails such as iteration limits.

questions.prompt: Your MCP server runs on the user's laptop, and the host app launches it as a child process. Which transport is this, and which rule does the spec set for it?

choices.text: stdio; the server must not write anything to `stdout` that is not a valid MCP message
stdio; the server writes its logs to `stdout` so the client can display them
Streamable HTTP; the client must first open a GET stream to receive messages
Streamable HTTP; the server must listen on `0.0.0.0` so the host can reach it

questions.explanation: In the stdio transport the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over `stdin` and `stdout`. `stdout` carries only MCP messages; logging goes to `stderr`. A stray `print()` to `stdout` corrupts the stream. The spec says a local Streamable HTTP server should bind only to localhost, not `0.0.0.0`.

sources.title: stdio - Model Context Protocol specification (2026-07-28)
sources.claim: In the MCP stdio transport the client launches the server as a subprocess, messages are newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout, the server MUST NOT write non-MCP output to stdout and MAY log to stderr.

sources.title: Streamable HTTP - Model Context Protocol specification (2026-07-28)
sources.claim: The Streamable HTTP spec says a locally running server SHOULD bind only to localhost rather than 0.0.0.0.

questions.prompt: You host one MCP server on the internet for many users, using Streamable HTTP. Which of these is a security requirement in the spec for that transport?

choices.text: Send every message as a newline-delimited line on the server's `stdout`
Use the HTTP+SSE transport from 2024-11-05, because more clients support it
Validate the `Origin` header on incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding
Keep one open TCP socket per user instead of sending messages as HTTP POSTs

questions.explanation: The Streamable HTTP spec says servers MUST validate the `Origin` header to prevent DNS rebinding, SHOULD bind to localhost when running locally, and SHOULD authenticate every connection. Each client message is its own HTTP POST to a single MCP endpoint. HTTP+SSE is deprecated, and newline framing on `stdout` belongs to stdio. The spec is versioned: the 2026-07-28 revision also removed protocol-level sessions and the GET stream, so check which revision your SDK implements.

sources.title: Streamable HTTP - Model Context Protocol specification (2026-07-28)
sources.claim: The Streamable HTTP spec says servers MUST validate the Origin header to prevent DNS rebinding, SHOULD bind to localhost locally and SHOULD authenticate; each client message is its own POST, HTTP+SSE is deprecated, and revision 2026-07-28 removed the GET stream and protocol-level sessions.
